clue.text: It's impossible to manufacture a bird

parts.note: to forge is to make or manufacture, as in a smithy
a tit is a small songbird

explanation.surface: A complaint that nobody could ever build a bird in a factory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's impossible' reads as the start of a sentence, but it is the whole definition, a curt refusal.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'forget it' is a colloquial way of declaring that something simply cannot happen or will never be done.

clue.text: Almost slice up rat

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
in a down clue, going up means reading the letters from bottom to top

parts.note: a knife slices; almost all of the word is kept

explanation.surface: Instructions for nearly cutting up a rodent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slice' is the tool that slices, KNIFE, with its last letter removed and then turned upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A fink is American slang for an informer, just as a rat is someone who betrays associates to the authorities.

clue.text: Joplin composition: a Bollywood soundtrack tune

parts.note: Scott Joplin wrote ragtime pieces, called rags
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Scott Joplin piece turning up as a song in an Indian film.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon suggests the definition follows the wordplay whole, but the 'a' belongs to the wordplay and the definition starts after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A raga is a melodic framework of Indian classical music, widely used in Indian film songs.

clue.text: Tesla rival is done screwing around

indicators.note: fooling about with no fixed order, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Gossip that the rival of Nikola Tesla, or the car company, has stopped messing about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tesla' suggests the modern car maker, but the rival meant is the inventor; 'screwing' also nods to light bulbs.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Edison battled Nikola Tesla in the 'war of the currents' over electrical power systems.

clue.text: Photo edges cropped from crude close-up pictures of ephemeral art

indicators.note: something crude is rough and unrefined, so the letters are put into a raw new order
cropping trims material away, so these letters are taken out
the edges of a word are its outermost letters, first and last

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word
taken as written

explanation.surface: A complaint about badly framed close-up photos of short-lived artworks.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove one P and the O from the fifteen letters of 'close-up pictures', then rearrange the remaining thirteen.
explanation.definitionFit: Carved ice melts away within hours or days, so these sculptures are a textbook example of art that does not last.

clue.text: Latest fake 'art' may be seen here

indicators.note: a fake is a made-up version, so the letters are rearranged into something new

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A gallery notice that the newest forged artwork is on show here.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotes round 'art' warn that it is not gallery art but the patterns baristas pour into milky coffees.
explanation.definitionFit: Latte art is the decorative leaf or heart drawn in steamed milk foam on top of a coffee.

clue.text: Sophocles heroine in favour of sticking around?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the title character of a Greek tragedy who buries her brother

definitions.note: a punning phrase read as 'anti-gone', not a true synonym
definitions.meaning: second meaning, punning: someone who wants to stay is against being gone

explanation.surface: A literary heroine who supports staying put.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the name as ANTI-GONE: being against having gone is being in favour of staying; the question mark flags the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Antigone is the protagonist of the tragedy by Sophocles, defying King Creon to bury her brother Polynices.

clue.text: Genteel affairs in which pirates ate bats

indicators.note: bats is slang for crazy, so the letters go wild and rearrange

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Polite gatherings where buccaneers dined on flying mammals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bats' looks like the food the pirates ate, but it is an adjective meaning crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: Tea parties are refined social occasions with cakes and fine china, the very picture of gentility.

clue.text: Get out of way of bear chased by first-string team?

parts.note: to bear something is to stand it, to put up with it
the A side is a club's first team

explanation.surface: Advice to dodge a bear that is being chased by a sports team's first eleven.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bear' is the verb meaning tolerate, not the animal; 'chased by' puts the team after it.
explanation.definitionFit: To stand aside is to step out of someone's path or withdraw so they can proceed.

clue.text: Removing bottom from lacy gown isn't half irresponsible

indicators.note: the bottom of a word written across is its end, so the final letter goes

parts.note: a negligee is a flimsy, often lacy nightgown

indicators.note: only half is kept, so the front half of the letters is discarded

parts.note: taken as written, without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Taking the bottom off a lace nightdress is somewhat reckless.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the last E of the nightgown, then keep only the back half of 'isn't'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe a careless failure to take proper care or meet one's duties.

clue.text: Wise monkeys count dogs in long baskets

parts.note: the proverbial wise monkeys see, hear and speak no evil, and there are three of them
pointers are gun dogs

explanation.surface: Monkeys tallying up dogs sitting inside large wicker baskets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long baskets' suggests wickerwork, but it means basketball shots made from distance.
explanation.definitionFit: In basketball, a shot scored from beyond the arc earns three points, so a long-range basket is a three-pointer.

clue.text: Bit of lightheartedness in western martial arts

indicators.note: in an across clue, heading west means reading from right to left
the letters sit inside the words that follow, spanning a gap

parts.note: the letters across the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: Some light comedy found in a cowboy kung-fu film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Western' looks like a film genre but tells you to read the run of letters backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Tra-la is a carefree sung refrain expressing gaiety, a small burst of cheerful high spirits.

clue.text: Squeezebox lost in a thousand pounds of Royal Albert Hall gear

indicators.note: what is lost is no longer there, so those letters drop out

parts.note: a concertina is a small accordion, nicknamed a squeezebox
the letters removed
a grand is slang for a thousand pounds or dollars

explanation.surface: An accordion goes missing among expensive equipment at a famous London venue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a' looks like a preposition placing the loss, but it is the letters lost from the end of the squeezebox. The Royal Albert Hall is London's great concert hall.
explanation.definitionFit: A concert grand is the largest grand piano, built for big halls, so it is standard equipment at a major venue.

clue.text: Great Hooters contests, stateside

parts.note: superb means great, excellent
owls hoot, so they are hooters

explanation.surface: Praise for competitions held at the Hooters restaurant chain in America.
explanation.walkthrough: Hooters is a US restaurant chain, but here the word means birds that hoot; the break falls inside SUPERB.
explanation.definitionFit: The Super Bowl is the annual championship game of American football, the biggest sporting contest in the United States.

clue.text: Able to contain it with internal force? It's conditional

indicators.note: having something internal means carrying it inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: continent describes a person able to control the bladder or bowels
G is the symbol for g-force

explanation.surface: A question about holding something in by force, answered with a remark on dependence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Able to contain it' sounds like a container, but it defines a whole word, the medical sense of self-control; G slips in after CONTIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Something contingent depends on another event happening first, so it is subject to a condition.

clue.text: Unexplained phenomena among retrograde moons of Uranus

indicators.note: retrograde motion goes backwards, so the letters run in the opposite direction
something among other things is in their midst, inside the words

parts.note: the run of letters spanning the three words

explanation.surface: Strange sightings near the backward-orbiting satellites of Uranus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retrograde' is a real astronomical term, which makes it a well-disguised reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Unidentified flying objects are sightings in the sky that nobody has managed to account for.

clue.text: Bench-sitters shift buttocks

parts.note: to shift is to change or alter
nates is the anatomical Latin for buttocks

explanation.surface: People on a bench moving their bottoms around.
explanation.walkthrough: NATES is an anatomical term solvers may not know.
explanation.definitionFit: In American sports, alternates are substitute players who wait on the sidelines bench until needed.

clue.text: You can see Venus with this device externally held by eccentric Yankee

definitions.text: You can see Venus with this

indicators.note: to be held is to be gripped inside, so one piece sits in another
eccentric means odd and off-centre, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the external letters of a word are its outside pair

parts.note: its first and last letters

explanation.surface: An odd American holds a gadget for viewing the planet Venus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This device' looks like a telescope, but the point is that no device is needed: Venus is visible unaided.
explanation.definitionFit: Venus is the brightest planet and is easily seen unaided, without binoculars or a telescope.

clue.text: Former wife's grip that'll need painkiller

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase, not a noun

parts.note: an ex is a former spouse
traction is grip on a surface

explanation.surface: An ex-wife's grip is so painful you'll need medication.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a description: a dental procedure that calls for anaesthetic.
explanation.definitionFit: Pulling a tooth at the dentist is painful, so it is normally done under local anaesthetic.

clue.text: Went to neaten garden

definitions.note: read as WEE'D, a past tense verb
definitions.meaning: first meaning: past tense of a nursery word for urinating, with an apostrophe in place of the missing letters
second meaning: to pull unwanted plants from a flowerbed

explanation.walkthrough: 'Went' looks like a simple journey, but 'to go' is also a euphemism for relieving oneself, written WEE'D.
explanation.definitionFit: Clearing unwanted plants tidies a flowerbed, and to wee is a colloquial word for urinating.

clue.text: Part of the head's religious centre

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the flat area at the side of the forehead
second meaning: a building for worship

explanation.surface: The headteacher's centre of worship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The head's' reads like a school head's possession, but 's means 'is', joining two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both the side of the skull beside each eye and a building dedicated to worship.

clue.text: One taking it to the edge fancifully guzzling rotten gin and a fifth of mulled wine?

definitions.text: One taking it to the edge fancifully guzzling rotten gin and a fifth of mulled wine?

indicators.note: to guzzle is to swallow greedily, so one piece takes others inside it

parts.words: One taking it to the edge fancifully
parts.note: an invented word, flagged as fanciful, for someone who goes to the brink

indicators.note: rotten things have decayed out of shape, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a fifth of ten letters is two, here the central pair

parts.note: the two middle letters of the ten

explanation.surface: A reckless type knocking back cheap gin and some mulled wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancifully' admits the container is a made-up word, one who goes to the brink. Read as a whole, the clue also describes the answer, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone downing rotten gin and mulled wine to excess, pushing their limits, is drinking heavily in one session.

clue.text: Lisa's brother is a spoiled brat!

indicators.note: something spoiled is damaged and messed up, so the letters are disordered

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A complaint that a girl's brother is an indulged little horror.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spoiled brat' is a stock phrase, so 'spoiled' passes as an adjective rather than an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: In the cartoon The Simpsons, Bart is the older brother of Lisa, both children of Homer and Marge.

clue.text: Chains raised in child's play

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising letters means reading them upwards
the letters lie within the words that follow

parts.note: the run of letters across the gap

explanation.surface: Chains being lifted during a children's game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chains' suggests metal links but means mountain ranges.
explanation.definitionFit: The Alps are a long system of mountain ranges in Europe, and a mountain chain is a connected line of peaks.

clue.text: Invitation word Don expressed?

indicators.note: what is expressed is spoken out, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

parts.note: to don clothes is to put them on and wear them

explanation.surface: A word that a man called Don says when inviting someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don' looks like a name or a university lecturer but is the verb meaning put on. Invitations state when and where.
explanation.definitionFit: Every invitation gives the venue, so the question word for place is a standard heading on one.

clue.text: Deep-sea swimming, both directions, for sunken gem

indicators.note: swimming things move about freely, so the letters drift into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, without the hyphen
L and R stand for left and right

explanation.surface: A diver swims every which way searching for a jewel lost on the seabed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Both directions' gives left and right, L and R, added to the anagram letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A seed pearl is a very small pearl, a gem found in oysters lying deep on the sea floor.

clue.text: Rover was one sort of dog

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Rover was the pseudonym of a Guardian crossword compiler
second meaning: a breed of gun dog, such as the Irish red

explanation.surface: Rover was a certain breed of dog.
explanation.walkthrough: Rover sounds like a dog's name, but it was a Guardian puzzle compiler's pseudonym.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a person who compiles crosswords and a long-haired breed of gun dog.

clue.text: Top Android, say, goes after toxic element in hazardous material

parts.note: As is the chemical symbol for arsenic
top means best
Android is an example of an operating system

explanation.surface: A leading robot follows a poisonous element into some dangerous substance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Android' looks like a robot, but it is the phone software, an operating system.
explanation.definitionFit: Asbestos is a fibrous mineral once used for insulation whose dust causes lung disease, a notorious health hazard.
